access.edition_or_version: First edition, U. Ray and Sons, Calcutta, 19 September 1923

mechanics.premise: 53 Bengali quatrains of nonsense verse, most composed for the children's magazine Sandesh between 1915 and 1923.
mechanics.point_of_view: A playful verse narrator who follows absurd premises to their logical ends without winking at the reader.
mechanics.invented_world_and_props: Compound creature-names (built by joining two ordinary animals) create new species that behave according to internally consistent absurd rules, functioning as props.
mechanics.play_frame: The book is self-aware as a nonsense game, its first and last poems sharing the title 'Abol Tabol'.
mechanics.style_and_devices: Portmanteau and neologism; faulty cause and effect played straight; reversals; aural suggestiveness; strict metre, rhyme, and syntax holding a base of sense.
mechanics.emotional_progression: Delight in invention sustained across short, self-contained poems rather than developed through narrative.
mechanics.dialogue: Dramatized monologues and reported speech in which characters reason calmly from impossible premises.
mechanics.conventions: Pioneered literary nonsense in Bengali literature, often compared to Carroll and Lear.
mechanics.innovation_or_subversion: Uses nonsense to embed subversive and anti-colonial meanings beneath children's verse, while its whimsy is valued as a positive aesthetic in its own right.
mechanics.critical_reception: Considered a nonsense masterpiece of Bengali literature; recent scholarship emphasizes the complexity of its humour beyond colonial satire.
mechanics.audience_reception: Beloved across generations in Bengal and the Bengali diaspora; continuously translated and anthologized.
